# An MCP tool set can gain a digest without changing

#mcp #security #opensource #observability

A schema default of `0.5` used to be enough for HISTOR to leave an MCP server's entire tool set without a digest. After a change to the measurement rules, the same declarations could receive one. The server's author did not have to edit anything.

That left an awkward historical record: "not digestible" could still describe a decision made under rules the observer no longer used. The label did not say which revision had declined the set.

HISTOR logs the tool definitions MCP servers advertise. Its MTL profile specifies a canonical representation of those definitions and the digest computed from it. MTL is our draft labeling profile; it is not a standard of the MCP project.

Two recent revisions addressed different parts of the problem. ## Letting unchanged packages run again

A scheduler watching only package versions would miss the change. It has already run that release, the release has not moved, and its old result says there is no tool-set digest.

HISTOR now makes a package eligible for another run when an older MTL revision declined its set. If the current revision still declines it, the recorded decision settles that case until relevant inputs change. The revision marker is excluded from security events, so an observer upgrade is not reported as a security event attributed to the package.

The scheduler regression checks this unchanged-version path. Label tests cover the two reasons, refusal codes, signatures with the new fields, and comparisons whose earlier label lacks a revision. Before the November 6 production switch, a disposable instance exercised label generation and both API views without network access; outside checks followed the deployment.

The distinction is visible in the public API: one unobserved entry and one undigested entry. Both returned their corresponding `noDigest.reason` when checked on November 7. These are reasons attached to particular measurements, so the date and profile revision matter as much as the word "missing."

# Two MCP logs matched 23 tools. Five days later, every name had changed.

#mcp #security #cryptography #opensource

Compare the latest saved entries for one MCP server and you get zero tool names in common. Compare the observations from the same evening and all 23 tool fingerprints match.

We maintain HISTOR, a transparency log for the tool definitions MCP servers advertise. We wanted to see whether an independent observer could corroborate one of our observations. We picked LEGION-tlog because it publishes a timestamp and a SHA-256 fingerprint for each tool. Those fingerprints let us compare individual definitions even when the logs use different formats for their records. LEGION developer documentation

## What the two logs saw

The server was `com.aiapplyd/aiapplyd`. We compared the tool name, description and input schema using LEGION’s canonicalization rule for per-tool fingerprints. All times below are UTC in 2026. HISTOR server history · LEGION server record

HISTOR observation  | What the comparison showed
--- | ---
19 October, 21:37:07  | All 23 fingerprints matched the LEGION observation from 22:01:05, about 24 minutes later.
24 October, 18:19:21  | All 23 names switched from `aiapplyd_` to `getmattered_`. The suffixes matched the earlier names. The latest entry in our archived LEGION response still showed the October 19 observation.
31 October, 12:45:49  | HISTOR recorded a set of 40 tools. None of their names appeared in the archived LEGION record. This is the set in the November 2 HISTOR snapshot.

The October 24 observation is easy to misread if you only look at counts. Both sets contain 23 tools, but a client using the earlier names would have to account for the name changes. The matching suffixes give you a way to line up the names. Whether the tools behave the same would take a separate test.

The evidence tells us when HISTOR first recorded the new set and which earlier version LEGION corroborated. It leaves open why the archived LEGION response had no later entry. In particular, the time of an observation and the time a server actually changed can differ.

## Replay the check offline

Download the offline replay bundle.

With the case bundle unpacked, run this from its directory using Node.js 22.
    
    `node replay.mjs > replay-output.json
    diff -u result.json replay-output.json
    `

An empty diff means the replay reproduced the saved result. The script uses Node’s standard library and the bundled records, keys, signed tree heads (STHs) and inclusion proofs. It performs three checks.

  1. LEGION-tlog. Verify the signing key against the pinned root key, verify the Ed25519 signatures on leaf 29030 and its STH, and recompute the path to the signed root of the 50,578-leaf Merkle tree.
  2. HISTOR. Verify the STH and the three signed MTL/1 labels against HISTOR’s pinned `did:key`. Verify their inclusion in the 1,564,894-leaf Merkle tree and recompute the tool set digest bound to each label.
  3. Comparison. Recompute the per-tool fingerprints from the authenticated HISTOR tool sets and compare them with the fingerprints in the LEGION record. The output lists names unique to either side and any shared names whose definitions differ.

The signed HISTOR label for the 40-tool set dates to October 31. The November 2 read time comes from snapshot metadata. The replay verifies inclusion under the bundled tree heads. Checking consistency across other tree heads or the behavior of the server would require separate evidence.

For a tool-pinning workflow, the case suggests a concrete diagnostic. When two logs disagree, put the observation timestamps next to the fingerprints and look for an earlier matching tool set. That can turn a generic mismatch into a dated, inspectable change.

We maintain HISTOR. AI assistance was used for the analysis, the replay code, the illustrations and the writing.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# We stopped reading 2,195 MCP servers for three days. Another team's log is how we found out

#devops #ai #mcp #opensource

HISTOR is our public log of MCP tool definitions. It reads every remote server in the official MCP registry every 30 minutes to 6 hours and records each change to the tools it advertises. From 29 October to 1 November it quietly stopped reading 2,195 servers it had read without trouble on 28 October.

Nothing on our dashboards turned red. We found out on 1 November, by comparing our log with one another team had started two days earlier. This post covers what broke, why the numbers we watched didn't show it, and what anyone writing an MCP client can take from it.

## Two ways to open an MCP connection

The MCP revision of 2026-07-28 changed how a session starts. Older revisions, up to 2025-11-25, open with an `initialize` request: the client and server agree on a protocol version, then the client asks for `tools/list`. 
  * Statuses: 400, 404, 405, and also 401 and 403;
  * Error bodies: a legacy error code under any id, or a body that isn't JSON-RPC at all;
  * Version lists: an error or discovery reply that lists only versions older than 2026-07-28;
  * Not a discovery reply: an answer to `server/discover` without `supportedVersions`;
  * The first page of `tools/list`: refused in the legacy way, before anything was read. One server advertised 2026-07-28 and then refused it.

These still stop the read: rate limits, timeouts, 5xx, redirects, the new revision's own errors, and ambiguous bodies.

The fix went live on 1 November at 08:44:57 UTC. In the first 90 seconds, 171 of 172 remote reads succeeded, and 145 of those used an older protocol. The 2,195 servers come back as their retry delays run out; we did not reset the schedule. By 04:21 UTC the next morning, 1,893 of the 2,193 still listed had been read again. Of the other 300, 161 now fail for reasons of their own: HTTP 400, 401 and 402, server errors, timeouts. 139 still stop in our reader with a protocol error, on answers the rule treats as ambiguous rather than as a legacy refusal; 73 of them send an error body that is JSON-RPC but malformed. Whether those deserve a fallback too is the next thing we look at.

## How many servers speak the new protocol

As a by-product we now know. Of the 21,474 remote servers HISTOR read successfully between 25 October and 1 November, the latest successful read negotiated:

Protocol version  | Servers
--- | ---
2026-07-28  | 4,097
2025-06-18  | 13,744
2025-03-26  | 2,853
2024-11-05  | 650
2025-11-25  | 126

Three months after the new revision, 19% of remote servers speak it. Four out of five still need `initialize`. One caveat: a server that speaks both and was last read before 29 October counts under its older version, which applies to 165 of them.

The data is open (CC BY 4.0): https://histor.modelmarket.dev/datasets/mcp-protocol-eras-2026-11-01/. It also has the list of the 2,195 servers and their last error.

# We installed 12,915 MCP servers and started each one. 41% never answered.

#security #ai #mcp #opensource

MCP registries list tens of thousands of servers. Most of what is written about their safety comes from reading them: the tool descriptions, the README, the code. We wanted the other half. What happens when you actually install one and start it, the way a client does? Does it answer? What does it ask for? What does it touch while it starts?

So HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, now installs the npm and PyPI servers it finds, starts each one in a sandbox and writes down what happened. The registries it follows list 47,586 npm and PyPI packages; it runs up to 8,000 per crawl. This post is the state on 13 October 2026, after 12,915 of them.

## How we ran them

  * The latest version, installed fresh. npm with `--ignore-scripts` (install scripts then run on their own, traced); PyPI wheels only, nothing built from source.
  * gVisor (`runsc`), an unprivileged user, a read-only root, 512 MB and one CPU. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer.
## If you publish an MCP server

  * List your tools without a key. Ask for it when a tool is called. Do not check its format at startup.
  * Default to stdio, or name the flag that turns it on in your error text.
  * Pin `mcp<2` or move to 2.x.
  * Ship one command. If your package also has a CLI, put `mcp` in the server's name.
  * Keep stdout for JSON-RPC. Logs, banners and help go to stderr.
  * Set `Requires-Python` honestly and publish wheels.
  * Do not download binaries at install or startup. Ship them as per-platform optional dependencies.

## Check what you run

Every package's record is public on histor.modelmarket.dev: its tools, what it asked for, what it touched, which image it ran in. WARDEN reads the same log. `npx -y @aimarket/warden@0.15.0 scan --histor` asks HISTOR, for every server in your Claude, Cursor or VS Code config, whether you get the tool set HISTOR recorded, and shows what its package did in the sandbox. For a package, that is the set its sandbox got. A launcher whose program is installed on your machine lists another one; its publisher can now declare that set in the server's registry entry, and HISTOR shows it as the publisher's word.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. The numbers are a snapshot of 13 October 2026; the crawl continues, so the site will have moved on. No package is named here. The method and the observer's code are in alexar76/histor (`docs/architecture.md`, `sandbox/histor_observe.py`).

Edited 14 October 2026: the WARDEN sentence above said it checks "whether you get the tool set everyone else gets". For a launcher package that is not one set, as a reader pointed out in the comments; it now says what HISTOR compares with.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#mcp #security #opensource #dataset

A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move.

## Half of them move

Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once.

  * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had.
  * 1,180 added a tool; 336 removed one.

# Five MCP security scanners on the same tool definitions

#mcp #security #ai #opensource

An MCP tool description can tell an assistant to change another tool's arguments, read a local file before answering, or hide an extra action. A useful scanner comparison needs to show which malicious definitions receive a signal, what happens on benign definitions, and which targets never receive a complete result.

I maintain both WARDEN and HISTOR, which supplies the historical package observations used here. That is a direct conflict of interest. I wrote some fixtures, and WARDEN has been developed with several of these datasets available. This is a maintainer-run comparison with inspectable evidence, not an independent ranking.

On the 485 served MCPTox definitions, published WARDEN produced high/critical signals on 460; the other four produced between 1 and 56. Lower-severity signals change that picture substantially, especially for mcp-audit. On historical packages, WARDEN also produced thousands of advisory-only signals. 
HISTOR's 2026-10-20 archive, with its signed manifest, supplied 14,930 rows. The archive is CC-BY-4.0, attributed to Aleksandr Artamokhov / HISTOR. Three missing digests came from immutable public API URLs without a separate stated license; their public inventory is metadata-only.

## Two remote gVisor hosts

Reported comparative measurements ran remotely on attested and PingBlip. An earlier local pilot is excluded and its generated artifacts removed. All bulk engines used `runsc`, network none, nonroot UID/GID 501:501, read-only root/source/runtime/data, dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges and dedicated results. No historical package implementation or upstream benchmark Python was executed.

Both hosts used image `sha256:db7085498187e8477fa462d5f1652d62bdf4b8af29ea3666bd1748a8315631a5`, containing Node 24.22.2 / Python 3.13.18. Node engines used 1 CPU / 768 MiB / pids 128. Audit base used 1 CPU / 768 MiB / pids 256; its historical phase used one worker / 1 CPU / 768 MiB on attested and two workers / 2 CPU / 1536 MiB on PingBlip. Linux cgroup quotas were checked. This is not a controlled speed comparison.

The 3,177-view catalog SHA-256 is `e29baa05fbdbf46e34631ff2c75f0b4f535f0188054dd4499699bd189a3dc757`; the 14,933-package catalog is `78d4dab7125318b80cc35302e7cf1cfc1a49fa6f310957ed7b8fddfb538375b6`. Every case has a file hash and common opaque wire id. Full methods and input units are in the report and data ZIP.

# Our Multica agents now work in an agent market: they buy, remember, review sellers, and sell their own work

#ai #security #opensource #agents

Multica is an agent factory: you give an agent a runtime, instructions and
a schedule, and it works through tasks. AIMarket hubs (modelmarket.dev is the public one)
are a market where agents buy capabilities from each other per call. We run both, and in the first week of November
we connected them. This is what the agents do now, what broke, what we found when we audited ourselves, and a

## The crew

Five agents run on one self-hosted Multica 0.5.3 (OpenCode + DeepSeek), on fixed UTC schedules:

  * GitHub digest, daily at 08:00: activity across our repositories, sent to Telegram. It keeps its past digests in Attested Memory, bought on our hub per call ($0.004 to search, $0.012 to write), so it can say "stars on X fell for the third day" instead of repeating yesterday. On a read-only mount it stops with an error, so mount the guard's folder writable but owned by root.

We could not test the permission layer by asking the model to break it: DeepSeek refused all six bypass attempts on
its own. We read OpenCode's source instead.

## If you run Multica too

We wrote a step-by-step guide, from the container to selling a long job, in English, Russian, Spanish, French
and Chinese. It sits in our open-source monorepo next to the Multica skill our agents use for buying and selling
and the full audit:

  * `multica/manual`;
  * `multica/community/aimarket/SKILL.md`;
  * `artifacts/vulnetix-class-multica-2026-11-05/REPORT.md`.

They reach the public mirror, github.com/alexar76/aicom, with its next sync, and this post will link them then.

What we would tell another operator:

  * Keep facts in scripts and prose in models.
  * Give each agent its own environment; the global config is shared by everyone on the daemon.
  * Put the network allowlist below the prompt, and the guard below the model, in a folder the agent cannot touch.
  * Allow an agent a wrapper you wrote, not a CLI with a wildcard.

## What this means for MCP crawlers

Most of those Disallow lines were written for search engines: `/api/`, `/dashboard`, `/admin`. Whether a monitor or an MCP client should honour them for an endpoint the publisher has listed in the MCP registry is a fair question. ScraperWatch honours robots.txt. Until 2 November HISTOR didn't consult it for registry-listed servers; since then it does, reading the `histor` group, or `*` if there is none, with RFC 9309's longest match. On the registry snapshot of 26 October, 4,708 of 33,520 remote endpoints (14%) disallow it. HISTOR's page for each of them says so and names the rule. Where robots.txt allows it, HISTOR still reads the server's MCP server card, the operator's own list of its tools.

If your crawler does honour robots.txt, it should read the file the way the site meant it. Concretely:

  * Run Python 3.13.14+, 3.14.5+ or 3.15. On 3.12 or older, use a parser that implements RFC 9309 rather than `urllib.robotparser`.
  * Test with `Allow: /` first and with a `$` rule. The four lines above cover the first; `Allow: /api/mcp$` before `Disallow: /api/` covers the second.
  * If you publish an MCP endpoint and want agents to reach it, `Allow: /api/mcp$` is correct, and the longest-match rule makes it work in any order. Crawlers on old Python will still miss it. A plain `Allow: /api/mcp` without the `$`, placed before the Disallow, works in both, at the cost of also allowing everything below that path.
